body: I changed only mergeIntervals, leaving the other seven exports byte-for-byte identical to the champion. The champion's mergeIntervals time (89 µs per call for 500 intervals) is dominated by `list.sort((a,b)=>a[0]-b[0])`, which pays for roughly 4500 JavaScript comparator invocations each doing two property loads on 2-element arrays; the actual merge scan is only a few microseconds. The new implementation packs each interval's (start, original index) into a single exactly representable double key `key = (start-min)*mult + i` (mult = smallest power of two ≥ len), sorts the Float64Array natively with no callbacks, recovers the index with an exact power-of-two floor/multiply, and then applies the champion's exact merge rule (`s <= curEnd` merges touching or overlapping intervals, otherwise a new interval starts). The fast path is taken only when every start is an int32 and the key magnitude stays below 2^53; otherwise the champion's comparator-based implementation is preserved verbatim in a helper, so semantics, output shape (plain 2-element arrays, ascending by start), and input immutability are unchanged.
